data.title: Testing for Independence in Two-Way Tables
data.description: Practice calculating expected joint probabilities under the assumption of independence and comparing them to observed frequencies across multiple real-world contingency tables.

challenges.question: If Teen and Rock were independent, the expected joint probability would be P(Teen) × P(Rock). Compute this expected joint probability (round to 2 decimals).
If 30 and over and Brand A were independent, the expected joint probability would be P(30 and over) × P(Brand A). Compute this expected joint probability (round to 2 decimals).
challenges.hint: P(30 and over) = 60/120 = 0.5. P(Brand A) = 57/120 = 0.48. Multiply.

challenges.question: If Grade 6 and Packed were independent, the expected joint probability would be P(Grade 6) × P(Packed). Compute this expected joint probability (round to 2 decimals).
If Over 1 mile and Walks were independent, the expected joint probability would be P(Over 1 mile) × P(Walks). Compute this expected joint probability (round to 2 decimals).

data.educationalContext: Assessing whether two categorical variables are independent is a fundamental statistical tool used to determine if an association or relationship exists between them in a given population.
